title: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
description: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them. AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts. They must do more to ensure safety. That’s why EU regulators and US agencies are rightfully calling for agent developers and deployers to monitor agents in real time. But these rules assume that companies can see what their agents are doing and why—when in reality, they lack sufficient visibility. Imagine a bank hiring a thousand new employees who can access customer accounts and sensitive information, but the employees’ ID badges change every day, it’s not clear whether a manager ever reviewed or authorized their work, and nobody logs the changes employees make to approval processes. That lack of visibility is where we are with agents today. As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine , we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent wide-ranging and potentially devastating consequences. And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability : the capacity to capture what the system did, process it into signals, and present those to humans or automated oversight systems. In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. And as our recent research shows, current agent frameworks—the software that runs agents— do not reliably generate the crucial observability records we need to ensure that agents are deployed safely. Agents present new kinds of problems that generative AI alone does not. They inherit the unpredictability of the LLMs they are built on, but where a generative AI system produces a single output for a human to act on, an agent performs longer tasks—it plans, picks tools, spawns sub-agents, and takes actions. So an agent’s course can take shape in a multitude of different ways, and no tests before launch can fully anticipate the risks. This makes observing the agents while they work even more challenging, and even more important. With colleagues from academia, civil society, and industry, we studied the four most widely used agent frameworks to see what signals they actually emit. We found major gaps that made it hard to achieve key safety goals, like noticing policy violations, unauthorized actions, and even human oversight failures. Key observability requirements were missing—like Agent IDs that persist over time, and records about which humans approved agent tasks. This made it hard to tell which agents did what or assess whether they were taking unauthorized actions. The good news is that these gaps, once identified, can be closed. Doing so starts with capturing two types of records: those that reveal what happened in an agent’s run and how the agent made its decisions. The “what happened” records identify the agent (while preserving privacy) and log how humans intervened and whether agent permissions or “memory” shifted, while the “decision” records show an agent’s reasoning and levels of confidence in the actions it’s taken. Take, for example, agents working to process a bank’s mortgage loans. The system examines an application and recommends denying it, and then a human loan officer signs off on the decision. In a later audit, or perhaps even in real time, a bank or regulator needs to be able to reconstruct which agent made the call, which officer approved it, and how long they took. And the bank must also analyze records of how the agent arrived at its refusal decision in order to ensure it did not use off-limits information, like details about the neighborhood the applicant is from. Recording “what happened” and “how the agent decided” require different approaches, but both are feasible. The current lack of “what happened” records is mostly a software plumbing problem that can be addressed through OpenTelemetry, an open observability standard maintained by engineers across the industry and by the agent frameworks adopting it. OpenTelemetry has launched a working group drafting shared formats for tracing agents, but they have yet to be finalized . The group should urgently incorporate standards for maintaining persistent agent identity and for recording human interventions and changes to agents’ permission or memory. And it should be done before these systems can scale, all the while attending to the privacy implications of agent ID that links to real people. Preserving “how agents decided” records is more challenging. The issue raises open research questions for model providers and researchers: Does the step-by-step reasoning a model displays, known as chain of thought, reflect how the model actually made a decision? And do we have reliable ways to measure how confident the agent is in that decision? These questions need answers before anyone sets standards for how such observability records are used. No single organization or sector can close the observability gaps on their own, but together, they can support the infrastructure required to prevent dangerous incidents and support safety. AI developers building agent frameworks, like OpenAI, Anthropic, CrewAI, and LangChain, must integrate telemetry signals recording an agent’s persistent identity, any human interventions, and any changes to an agent’s permissions and memory. Meanwhile, enterprises adopting these agent frameworks have an influential role to play; enterprises in regulated industries, like banks and hospitals, can put pressure on the agent developers to supply these missing observability records where standards do not yet exist. Enterprises must also define policies, permissions, and roles that set out what agents can safely do, since telemetry alone cannot assess whether agents broke specific rules. Finally, regulators and AI standards institutes must specify the observability records required for high-stakes AI deployments while leaving the technical details to industry. We have already seen initial momentum here: NIST’s agent standards initiative in the US is working on agent identity, one of the most salient gaps we found in our research. No bank would let a thousand unbadged employees loose on customer accounts and hope to piece together what happened when something goes wrong. Yet that’s how we’re deploying AI agents. Making their behavior observable is the first step toward fixing this. And by building the regulatory and policy ecosystem that makes it possible to act on what we see, we can hold organizations accountable. Until then, every task we hand to an agent hands over our agency, too. Madhulika Srikumar is the Head of the AI Safety Program at the Partnership on AI, a global non-profit partnership of leading industry, academic, and civil society organizations, advancing best practices in AI governance. Claire Leibowicz is the Director of AI, Trust, and Society at the Partnership on AI and a doctoral candidate at Oxford University.

title: AWS will be a $1T business, Jassy says — but first, it will spend big
description: Amazon wants to be the king of AI cloud computing and become the first $1 trillion revenue business. But to do that it will have to continue on its capex spending spree, its CEO said Thursday.
content: Andy Jassy has made it known that he believes AWS can be a trillion-dollar revenue business. During Amazon’s quarterly earnings call on Thursday, he repeated this ambition. “What we’re building at Amazon is unlike anything that’s ever been seen before. There has never been a business with a trillion dollars of annual revenue,” he said. However, before the cloud business gets there, Amazon is going to have to ramp up its capital expenditures to build out the infrastructure necessary to support that blossoming business. “We still expect 2026 cash capex of approximately $220 billion — the majority for AWS — and expect to spend meaningfully more in 2027, with a clear line of sight to attract its financial returns,” Jassy revealed on Thursday. Amazon’s big spending on its AI infrastructure buildout has been an ongoing source of concern for investors this year. Indeed, during Thursday’s call, Wall Street analysts repeatedly asked Jassy to explain the spending, the signals that the growth really will come, and the profit margins expected. Jassy told them it was all money well spent because the e-commerce giant planned to capitalize on a historic moment in global cloud demand driven by AI. AWS revenue increased 39% from the year-ago quarter, a trend of steady growth for the sixth straight quarter . And the CEO forecast that it would increase by 40% not just next year, but in 2028, too. “AWS is a $184 billion annualized revenue run-rate business, and yet the opportunity remains extraordinary,” Jassy enthused. “With our continued pace of innovation, new core and AI functionality, enterprises wanting to run their core and AI workloads in AWS, and the amount of capacity that we’re adding each year, we believe that AWS can grow north of 40% in each 2027 and in 2028, and be a trillion-dollar revenue business in the next five to 10 years.” Jassy added that the company was “in the very early days” of AI adoption by the enterprise and said that, so far, the “strategy is working.” Later, when questioned why the investment needed to grow AWS was so substantial, Jassy characterized the AI boom as a “once-in-a-lifetime opportunity” that required, and was worth, such a big financial commitment now. “We’re going to invest to continue being the leader,” he said. “We can fund this plan, and I think it will forever change the size of Amazon. It will forever change our revenue.” Investors, however, remained concerned. Shares were down about 6% on Thursday in after-market trading. The AI boom has been a mixed blessing for the cloud industry, since the AI services that undergird the boom are supported by cloud infrastructure. Like Amazon, other cloud providers are spending big but also earning big. Microsoft, for instance, just posted yet more record-breaking revenue growth, driven largely by its cloud business. It, too, has spent a bundle . Topics AI , Amazon , AWS , Enterprise When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. title: Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face
content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face Published October 29, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 47 +41 merve merve Follow Alvaro Bartolome alvarobartt Follow Rémi Ouazan Reboul ror Follow Cyril Vallez cyrilvallez Follow Quentin Gallouédec qgallouedec Follow Enrique Hernández Calabrés ehcalabres Follow Juan Julián juanjucm Follow Xuan-Son Nguyen ngxson Follow Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow Aritra Roy Gosthipaty ariG23498 Follow :last-child]:mb-0"> Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter , and a context window of 1M tokens . The model is released in two official variants: FP8 NVFP4 There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings). Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more! Table of Contents "Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face" Table of Contents What is new with Mistral Large 4 Cybersecurity Capabilities Architecture Vision encoder Benchmark Results Inference Support Transformers vLLM Llama.cpp Fine-tuning with TRL Inference Endpoints Dell Enterprise Hub Try it out What is new with Mistral Large 4 Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions. You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection . Cybersecurity Capabilities Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for. Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model. For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description. In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community. We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here . Architecture Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query. For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers. The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token. Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope , a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency. Vision encoder Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below. Benchmark Results Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index. On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1 , 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA , and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4 . Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max. Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase , which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks. Cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance: Artificial Analysis Cyber Index: ML4 ranks among the top five models globally on this independent evaluation of models’ ability to find and fix software vulnerabilities. Vulnerability reproduction and patching: It achieves 82% , the highest reported score on this test within the index. The task requires reproducing a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patching it, testing both investigation and remediation. Cybench: ML4 solves 93% of a suite of 40 challenges drawn from security competitions , demonstrating strong performance on hands-on security problems. Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark , adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation. Inference Support Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team . We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers. Transformers The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM , with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low , medium , high as reasoning effort. The default is high , and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort : none would still use high . To run the model, upgrade the transformers package pip install --upgrade transformers import os from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM, DistributedConfig distributed_config = DistributedConfig( tp_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), ep_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), ) model_id = "mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, distributed_config=distributed_config, ) # only text text_messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "Who are you?" } ] # text + image multimodal_messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "image" , "image" : "https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/cats-image/resolve/main/cats_image.jpeg" , }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "How many cats are in the image?" , }, ], }, ] for messages in [text_messages, multimodal_messages]: inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , reasoning_effort= "medium" , ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 100 ) if int (os.environ[ "RANK" ]) == 0 : print (processor.decode(outputs[ 0 ][input_len:], skip_special_tokens= False )) You can run the script above by saving it in a python file script.py and then run torchrun --nproc-per-node 8 script.py vLLM vLLM supports the high-quality NVFP4 Mistral Large 4 checkpoint, which has a smaller memory footprint and requires NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. The model also ships with a DSpark drafter for additional speed-ups with vLLM. Launch the server like this: vllm serve mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-NVFP4 \ --config-format mistral \ --load-format mistral \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --decode-context-parallel-size 8 \ --enable-expert-parallel \ --dtype bfloat16 \ --max-model-len 131072 \ --max-num-seqs 16 \ --max-num-batched-tokens 2048 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --enforce-eager \ --mm_processor_cache_gb 0.0 Once the server is up and running, you can run the following. curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"What is 17*23?"}],"max_tokens":512}' Llama.cpp Llama.cpp and Llama App already support Mistral Large 4. You can install Llama App with the following command: curl -LsSf https://llama.app/install.sh | sh Then you can start the server as follows, indicating the quant suffix after the model ID: llama serve -hf ggml-org/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-GGUF:Q2_K Here’s the repository with the quants derived from the FP8 checkpoint, and this is the NVFP4 one , converted from the official NVFP4 repo. Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat using the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever. You can also query the server as follows. Feel free to check out the API reference for multimodality, tool calls and more. curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."}, {"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about python exceptions"} ] }' You can run image-text inference as follows. curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer " \ -d '{ "model": "muse-spark-open", "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": [ { "type": "text", "text": "What is in this image?" }, { "type": "image_url", "image_url": { "url": "data:image/png;base64,..." } } ] } ], "temperature": 0 }' The llama.cpp team ships the following quants: IQ2_XXS , Q2_K , Q4_K_M , NVFP4 , Q8_0 , and BF16 for further conversions. The 2-bit quants run on a single Apple Silicon Ultra computer with 512 GB of unified RAM. The others require distributed inference. You can also run on multiple NVIDIA or AMD cards. Running Q2_K on a single M3 Ultra, we got a prefill throughput of about 90 tokens per second, and a generation speed of 15 tok/s. On 4 x RTX6000 Pro, we observed the following results: NVFP4: 32K context size, prefill 130-590 t/s, gen speed ~10 t/s IQ2_XXS: 800K context size. At short context sizes, prefill is 500 tok/s and generation runs at 30 tok/s. However, using long contexts performance drops to 129 tok/s (prefill) and 3 tok/s (generation). Fine-tuning with TRL We also ship day 0 support of fine tuning Mistral Large 4 using TRL. All you have to do is upgrade to the latest version of transformers , trl and peft . pip install --upgrade transformers trl peft In the following example we train the model to perform multilingual thinking. The fine tuned model would be able to reason in the language the system prompt asks for! The script runs on the FP8 variant on a node of 8xB300s. The full example, with a Slurm launcher, is in TRL's examples . # torchrun --nproc-per-node 8 sft.py import os from datasets import load_dataset from peft import LoraConfig from transformers import AutoModelForImageTextToText, DistributedConfig from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer world_size = int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]) model_id = "mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B" model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained( model_id, distributed_config=DistributedConfig(fsdp_size=world_size, ep_size=world_size), dtype= "auto" , ) dataset = load_dataset( "HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking" , split= "train" ) # the assistant turns carry reasoning, so render them in reasoning mode dataset = dataset. map ( lambda x: { "chat_template_kwargs" : { "reasoning_effort" : "high" }}) trainer = SFTTrainer( model=model, args=SFTConfig( packing= True , max_length= 4096 , assistant_only_loss= True , learning_rate= 1e-4 , lr_scheduler_type= "cosine" , warmup_steps= 10 , ), train_dataset=dataset, peft_config=LoraConfig( r= 16 , lora_alpha= 32 , target_modules= r".*language_model.*\.(q_proj|kv_a_proj_with_mqa|kv_b_proj|o_proj|gate_proj|up_proj|down_proj)" , ), ) trainer.train() Inference Endpoints Mistral Large 4 is also available on Inference Endpoints, with a ready-to-deploy recipe on 8 x NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The recipe runs vLLM with the FP8 weights split across all eight GPUs using tensor and expert parallelism, and uses the model's built-in DSpark draft head for faster generation through speculative decoding. It serves up to 131K tokens of context and processes up to 16 requests at a time, and we observed the following results: Single request: time to first token of about 0.6 seconds for a 1K-token prompt, and a generation speed of ~65 tok/s, reaching 120–138 tok/s on chat prompts where DSpark's drafts are accepted. Long prompts: 16K-token prompts, four at a time, are prefilled at about 4,300 tok/s in total, with a time to first token of 8–9 seconds. Under load: about 480 tok/s of total generation across 1,000 ShareGPT conversations. You can deploy it with the hf CLI as follows: hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B --name mistral-large-4 Once the endpoint is running, you can query its OpenAI-compatible API, using the endpoint URL and your Hugging Face token. The reasoning_effort field controls how much the model reasons before answering, and can be set to low , medium , or high (default). curl " $(hf endpoints describe mistral-large-4 --json | jq -r .status.url) /v1/chat/completions" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $(hf auth token 2>/dev/null) " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B", "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about python exceptions"} ], "reasoning_effort": "medium" }' The answer comes back in choices[0].message.content , and the reasoning in choices[0].message.reasoning . The endpoint also supports tool calls, structured outputs, image inputs, and streaming through the standard Chat Completions fields. Dell Enterprise Hub The easiest way to get up and running with your Dell AI Servers (NVIDIA H200, B200, GB200 or GB300) is by installing the dell-ai CLI: pip install dell-ai && dell-ai login And use it to run an optimized recipe for Mistral Large 4 on e.g., a NVIDIA B300 node. dell-ai models deploy --model-id mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-NVFP4 \ --engine docker \ --platform-id xe9780-nvidia-b300 \ --gpus 4 You can find more about this release in the Dell Enterprise Hub (DEH) . Try it out Grab the weights from the Mistral Large 4 collection , run them locally with the GGUFs , or deploy them with Inference Endpoints. We can't wait to see what you build with Le Chonk. Share your fine-tunes, quants and other artefacts on the Hub! title: Microsoft’s AI future has fewer jobs
description: To anyone listening closely to what Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been saying over the past couple of years, this week felt like the clearest sign yet that AI is about to fundamentally change the size of Microsoft's workforce. Microsoft is now offering voluntary buyouts to around 60,000 employees across the US, UK, Canada, and […]
content: Tech AI Gaming Microsoft’s AI future has fewer jobs It’s also time to name the next Elder Scrolls game, and Xbox’s architect of Forza Motorsport is leaving. It’s also time to name the next Elder Scrolls game, and Xbox’s architect of Forza Motorsport is leaving. by Tom Warren Oct 29, 2026, 4:00 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge Tom Warren is a senior correspondent and author of Notepad , who has been covering all things Microsoft, PC, and tech for over 20 years. To anyone listening closely to what Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been saying over the past couple of years, this week felt like the clearest sign yet that AI is about to fundamentally change the size of Microsoft’s workforce. Microsoft is now offering voluntary buyouts to around 60,000 employees across the US, UK, Canada, and India. It’s the first time the company has presented such an offer to so many employees, expanding greatly upon the retirement offer that was limited to around 9,000 employees earlier this year. It’s all part of an ongoing effort to avoid reducing investment in AI infrastructure by lowering Microsoft’s operating costs and headcount. “Our total people costs will go down, our cost per head will go up, and my GPU per researcher will go up,” Nadella said on a podcast almost two years ago, responding to a question about AI’s impact on headcount. That’s a financial way of saying Microsoft will have fewer people, but it will offer higher salaries and more tools and AI power to those who remain. It also helps explain the continued layoffs we’ve seen at Microsoft over the past couple of years. Microsoft has been performing layoffs regularly over the past decade, but over the past couple of years, the layoffs and executive departures have been significant. These aren’t the annual layoffs of old; they’re now happening every few months. This week’s voluntary exit offer arrived just months after Microsoft laid off 4,800 employees , cuts that impacted its Xbox and commercial sales teams the most. For the first time in a decade, Microsoft’s overall headcount has also gone down year over year . Microsoft now employs around 223,000 people as of June 30th, 5,000 fewer than the 228,000 people it employed in 2025. Microsoft laid off 4 percent of its workforce in July last year, and it’s now offering voluntary buyout offers to around a quarter of its employees. More than 30 percent of the 9,000 eligible employees accepted a retirement offer earlier this year, but that number will likely be far less for the company’s latest Voluntary Exit Offer. That’s largely because, according to sources familiar, the offer is practically the same as regular severance terms at Microsoft — cash based on time at the company, accelerated stock vesting, some additional subsidized health coverage, and several months of career services. But what makes this unusual is the scale of the amount of employees who have been offered this exit. Even if only 5 percent accept the offer, that’s still 3,000 employees. I understand eligible employees have until December to decide, so we won’t know the impact of this offer for a while yet. With rumors of more layoffs in November and January, the amount of employees who do accept will surely inform Microsoft’s numbers for its next round of cuts. There are some, both inside and outside the company, who think Microsoft needs these cuts. “Microsoft needs fewer people,” says Merill Fernando , a former Microsoft Entra product manager. “I’ve been on the inside. I’ve seen how things get built. Lots of small orgs. Layers on layers. Silos everywhere.” Fernando paints a picture of a Microsoft where every organization “had its own priorities and its own decision makers,” so it’s hard to get the company to do anything collectively. It sounds a little like the meme where each organization in Microsoft is pointing guns at each other, competing instead of collaborating. Nadella even addressed that meme last year in a podcast with Stripe co-founder John Collison , acknowledging that the comic has defined Microsoft’s cultural narrative “more so than reality,” but that it had signaled some very real tensions inside the company. “In some sense, some of these divisional tensions are real issues that need to have tension. Social cohesion is not a goal, winning in the marketplace is a goal,” said Nadella. The question now is whether Nadella can reshape Microsoft for the AI era without undoing the cultural transformation that helped define his leadership. A company that has shifted to be built around empathy is now asking its employees to reckon with an AI future that could make many of their jobs unnecessary. How Nadella handles that transition will define his legacy as much as the growth and success he’s achieved over the past decade. Xbox’s architect of Forza Motorsport is leaving after nearly 27 years A few weeks ago I started hearing from Xbox employees that Dan Greenawalt , the longtime creative force behind Forza Motorsport , is leaving after almost 27 years. Greenawalt is departing as the head of Turn 10 Studios, the Forza Motorsport creator that merged with Forza Horizon developer Playground Games. Playground Games studio head Trevor Williams revealed the news in a recent internal memo, seen by Notepad . “Dan Greenawalt has decided that this is the right time for him to retire from Microsoft,” says Williams. Greenawalt will stay on as an adviser to Williams and the newly appointed Playground Games chief operating officer, Michel Bastien, “while he transitions to his next phase.” Here’s part of Williams’ memo about Greenawalt: It’s hard to overstate Dan’s impact over the past 27 years. From shipping Project Gotham Racing on the original XBOX in 2001 to leading the creation of Forza, founding Turn 10 Studios and appearing so many times on our E3 stage, usually making a dramatic entrance with a supercar in tow – and so much more – we owe tremendous thanks and gratitude to Dan. On behalf of both teams, I would like to thank Dan for his leadership, his support, and his partnership. I wish him well for whatever comes next. Microsoft revealed last month that it was merging its two Forza developers into a single studio as part of a massive restructuring of Xbox . Both Playground Games and Turn 10 Studios have merged into just Playground Games. The studio now has two locations: Playground Games Leamington Spa and Playground Games Redmond. With Greenawalt retiring and Turn 10 merged into Playground Games, it’s not clear if we’ll ever see Microsoft return to Forza Motorsport . More than 70 people at Turn 10 Studios were laid off last year , in a move that hit the vast majority of the studio. Over the past year, Turn 10 Studios has essentially been maintaining Forza Motorsport , and now the remaining employees have moved to Playground Games to work on Forza Horizon and Fable . It’s time to name The Elders Scrolls VI: Sentinel It’s been more than eight years since Bethesda officially announced the existence of the sixth game in its Elder Scrolls series. While there have been some debates around platform exclusivity for The Elder Scrolls VI , we’ve heard very little detail about the game that Bethesda has been working on all this time. Sources familiar with Bethesda’s plans tell me that the Xbox-owned publisher is about to announce that the next Elder Scrolls game will officially be called The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel . The announcement could come as soon as next month, during a period that will mark 15 years since The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim was released. Bethesda has been showing off Sentinel gameplay in recent months, I’m told. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma got a live playthrough of Sentinel in August, and she praised the scale of the game and said “the story is even greater.” While I’m only expecting a name reveal next month and nothing more, I’ve been hearing some additional details about the game. If you want to totally avoid spoilers about the game, then don’t read the next paragraph. I understand that Sentinel will be set in Hammerfell, a province in the Elder Scrolls universe that’s appeared in The Elder Scrolls Adventures: Redguard and The Elder Scrolls Online . Sentinel will be the first game about the history of the Elder Scrolls, and help uncover the secrets of these mysterious ancient artifacts. The pad Xbox’s first chief operating officer is out after just a few months. This is a weird one. Helen Chiang is leaving Microsoft after 21 years . She previously served as the head of Minecraft before being promoted to Xbox COO in July. The sudden departure was announced in a surprisingly short memo from Xbox chief Asha Sharma last week. “Helen Chiang is leaving Microsoft today. I’m grateful for her years of service and wish her well,” says Sharma. It doesn’t seem like the Xbox COO position is going away, as Sharma notes that “we’ll share more on COO leadership as plans are finalized.” Eurogamer reported over the weekend that Chiang had been “terminated for policy violations.” I’ve heard similar chatter internally, but Chiang has been described to me by multiple Xbox employees as highly respected, with high integrity, so this turn of events is quite odd. I’m trying to get more details, but if you’ve heard anything, please reach out confidentially at notepad@theverge.com or through the secure Signal messaging app. ( I’m tomwarren.01 .) Microsoft’s new Surface Laptop Ultra update fixes reboot and display bugs. I ran into some weird issues with the Surface Laptop Ultra during my review, and Microsoft is now fixing some of them with a firmware update . The update addresses screen flickering, unexpected restarts, and lengthy reboot times alongside unspecified “additional bug fixes and general performance improvements.” I’m still waiting to see if Nvidia or Microsoft addresses the strange laggy feeling on the Surface Laptop Ultra, and it’s too early to say whether this firmware update addresses that or not yet. GitHub’s former CEO launched a competing platform for AI agents. We knew that Thomas Dohmke, former GitHub CEO, was building some kind of competitor to GitHub, but the result has surprised people internally during the week of GitHub’s Universe conference. Developers can use the new Entire platform to host and review code, but it’s also designed to work with AI agents and replaces pull requests with a “Trails” feature that offers “customizable evals that are scored by agents on every code push.” One GitHub employee tells me, “people are shocked, they have ambushed us up and down the stack on our own conference week.” Windows will soon let you perform an internet speed test without opening your browser. Microsoft added a speed test option to the Windows 11 taskbar earlier this year, but it was just a link to a speed test in Bing that opened in your browser. Now, Microsoft is actually integrating a full speed test into the taskbar , so you can right-click the network icon and perform an internet speed test right there. Windows 11 is getting some neat trackpad features. Microsoft is adding new Windows trackpad features that let you scroll through long documents and webpages faster. You’ll also be able to continuously scroll through a page by swiping the edge of your touchpad, along with support for single-finger scrolling. It’s the small things that count, and I love to see these kinds of features being added to Windows. Microsoft says its AI tool is better than doctors at diagnosing conditions. Microsoft claims to have developed an AI-powered tool that it says can diagnose conditions up to four times more accurately than human doctors . The findings were published last week in Science , one of the world’s most prestigious journals. Microsoft has pitted its AI system against human physicians on a series of scenarios drawn from medical case reports and emergency department data. While there’s still a long road ahead before this AI system can be widely deployed, Microsoft thinks its work is significant. “It needs clinical validation,” says Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman in an interview with The Verge . “That is a leap, but this is a major milestone along that journey.” Microsoft Authenticator flaw lets malicious Android apps steal tokens. Security researchers at Enclave have discovered a vulnerability with Microsoft Authenticator that lets an unprivileged Android app with zero permissions “impersonate any installed Microsoft first-party app and have the Microsoft Authenticator broker hand it that app’s tokens.” The tokens could provide full access to mailboxes, files, and calendars. Microsoft has now fixed the flaw, and if you use Microsoft Authenticator on Android, then it’s time to update it immediately. Denmark has abandoned plans to ditch Microsoft Office after technical problems. Last year the government of Denmark announced it was ditching Windows and Office in favor of open-source alternatives to reduce its reliance on US vendors. It seems like the trial of moving away from Microsoft’s software hasn’t gone too well for the Danish government, though. The Danish Ministry of Digitalisation has reportedly ended its trial for an open-source alternative to Microsoft Office. Employees reportedly encountered issues with document formatting, blank pages, and tracking changes. Gears of War: E-Day cost $500 million to make. Gears of War E-Day has the highest Metacritic score of any entry in the franchise since the Xbox 360 days, but it faces some tough questions around how much it costs to create a AAA game these days and what success looks like. Kotaku reports that E-Day cost “over $500 million” to make, excluding marketing budgets. This has generated a lot of discussion online over E-Day ’s success, especially as it’s a controversial test for any potential return to Xbox exclusivity. One source tells me that more than 400,000 copies of the game have been sold across Xbox and Steam, but the big question is whether Microsoft was happy with its Game Pass numbers for E-Day , and whether that revenue offsets any additional sales on Xbox and potential PS5 sales if a port had been released. Arkane Lyon and Blade could be about to be saved. Earlier this year, I reported that Microsoft was weighing up canceling its Blade game and shuttering Arkane. In the months since June, Microsoft has been in ongoing discussions with multiple publishers about a potential sale of Arkane Lyon amid consultations with the union representing the studio’s employees. French newspaper Le Monde now reports that Microsoft has a November 13th cutoff date for a decision on the future of Arkane Lyon, and Microsoft confirmed to PC Gamer that it’s extending this deadline by an additional month. An extension makes it seem like Microsoft is close to a deal, and I’m cautiously optimistic that Blade will be saved. We’ll find out in the coming weeks. Microsoft is ending Copilot support on smart TVs. After nearly two years of Copilot support on smart TVs, Microsoft is pulling the plug . I’d love to know how many people actually used Copilot this way, because it can’t be more than a dozen. LG says the Copilot TV feature is “scheduled for discontinuation during 2026” and a specific date is “subject to Microsoft’s timeline.” Microsoft reveals strong cloud growth amid financial reporting overhaul. Microsoft overhauled its financial reporting this quarter, placing Windows, Surface, and Xbox in a separate bucket to its more revenue generating AI and cloud efforts. Windows OEM revenue was down 22 percent amid a RAMageddon crisis that has seen the overall PC market drop by 20 percent in the recent quarter. Xbox hardware and content and services were also down, but a whole third of Microsoft’s revenue came from Azure ($33.17 billion of the $92.3 billion). I thought Nadella’s most interesting remarks on the earnings call were about Microsoft’s own AI models. “Our goal is to advance the cost to outcome frontier, which means delivering capabilities comparable to leading models within three to six months of their release at a fraction of the training cost, thereby allowing us to transfer those cost benefits to customers,” said Nadella. I’m always keen to hear from readers, so please drop a comment here, or you can reach me at notepad@theverge.com if you want to discuss anything else. If you’ve heard about any of Microsoft’s secret projects, you can reach me via email at notepad@theverge.com or speak to me confidentially on the Signal messaging app, where I’m tomwarren.01 . I’m also tomwarren on Telegram, if you’d prefer to chat there. Thanks for subscribing to Notepad . title: OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings acquires ADT
description: OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings is buying ADT in a $15.3 billion deal, with plans to bring AI to the home security business.
content: In Brief Posted: 12:56 PM PDT · October 29, 2026 Image Credits: Timon Schneider/SOPA Images/LightRocket / Getty Images Julie Bort OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings acquires ADT Thrive Holdings has acquired physical security company ADT for $10 per share or about $7.6 billion in equity, the companies announced on Thursday. Beyond equity, the total enterprise value of the deal is $15.3 billion, ADT said. Thrive Holdings is the holding company spinout from Josh Kushner’s powerhouse VC firm Thrive Capital. It also counts OpenAI as its partner , as well as an investor. The firm’s mission is to hold other companies long-term, revitalizing them with AI. Currently, Thrive Holdings holds over 75 companies, it says. As a partner, OpenAI supplies AI models and tech as well as people, otherwise known as forward-deployed engineers, to Thrive’s companies. Neither ADT nor Thrive announced what new AI-powered security products they will be releasing, but they did tease that the plan was to invest and release new products. “ADT will form the foundation of Thrive Holdings’ smart home security business,” the press release said. AI-powered physical security is having a moment right now. Apple just entered the field with a new line of smart home and home security products in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric. Amazon updated its smart home line, including new AI-powered home cameras . ADT already partners with Apple and Google and is expected to continue to do so. And who knows what the future might bring? Some startups are offering AI dog robots as roving security guards . Note: This story was updated to include ADT’s current partnerships and to describe Thrive Holdings as a holding company. title: Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready
content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready Published October 29, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 16 +10 Avijit Ghosh evijit Follow hfpolicy Sayeed Choudhury sayeedmd Follow CMU-OSPO Greg Tananbaum gtananbaum Follow ORCA-Open Emma Scharfmann EmmaScharfmann Follow hugging-science Georgia Channing cgeorgiaw Follow hugging-science Eunice Mercado-Lara EuniceML Follow ORCA-Open Irene Solaiman irenesolaiman Follow hfpolicy :last-child]:mb-0"> An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon. Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar , an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University , opens on November 2. See How to Participate below. The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University , Purdue University , Georgia Institute of Technology , Arizona State University , and The George Washington University , all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute ; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA) , through its Fostering Innovation Network , as the community partner. Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org . Making publicly funded science more usable The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development , and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data. But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines. Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI . The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release. The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains , including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models. The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025 , with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader. Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data . When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets . Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X . By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon. This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories. Open Science Challenges Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse. A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit? To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals: Demonstrate scientific reuse. Produce concrete examples of researchers and developers building on publicly funded scientific artifacts, including applications that combine resources across institutions or disciplines. Learn what makes reuse possible. Identify technical barriers, documentation gaps, interoperability challenges, and successful practices that can inform future research infrastructure, funding decisions, and public policy. The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful. The first challenge: Climate Risk Intelligence Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026 The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University , teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios. Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy. Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns. Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available. Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face . How to Join Project ProtoStar Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful. We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org . Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale. content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms Published October 29, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 10 +4 Mattt mattt Follow :last-child]:mb-0"> Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do. Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive. In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap , we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model. Today we're announcing two packages: AnySpeechRecognizer implements Apple's new speech-to-text API with a choice of recognition engine, including NVIDIA's Parakeet and Alibaba's Qwen3-ASR running locally on Core ML, and adds speaker diarization to track who speaks when. AnyDecisionModel answers yes-or-no, multiple-choice, and rating-scale questions with typed results and probabilities. It derives each answer from the model's probabilities instead of generating text, using a model on your device with MLX, Core AI, or llama.cpp, or a decision model from Jev or Ollama. Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device. AnySpeechRecognizer Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer , Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen. It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine: - import Speech + import AnySpeechRecognizer The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer , SpeechTranscriber , DictationTranscriber , SpeechDetector , and AssetInventory , with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber: let transcriber = SpeechTranscriber ( model: ParakeetSpeechModel (variant: .v3), transcriptionOptions: [], reportingOptions: [.volatileResults], attributeOptions: [.audioTimeRange] ) The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework. Meet the models Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 . It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale. Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3 . It was more accurate in most of our measurements. Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet . All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence. Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one: let transcriber = SpeechTranscriber ( model: QwenSpeechModel (variant: .large, language: Locale . Language (identifier: "yue" )), transcriptionOptions: [], reportingOptions: [], attributeOptions: [] ) Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input. To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started. Core ML models on the Hub To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub: Model Core ML conversion Original checkpoint License Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 mattt/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3-coreml nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3 CC BY 4.0 Parakeet Ultra mattt/parakeet-ultra-coreml moondream/parakeet-ultra CC BY 4.0 Parakeet Unified EN 0.6B mattt/parakeet-unified-en-0.6b-coreml nvidia/parakeet-unified-en-0.6b NVIDIA Open Model License Qwen3-ASR 0.6B mattt/qwen3-asr-0.6b-coreml Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-0.6B-hf Apache 2.0 Qwen3-ASR 1.7B mattt/qwen3-asr-1.7b-coreml Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-1.7B-hf Apache 2.0 Streaming Sortformer 4spk v2 mattt/diar-streaming-sortformer-4spk-v2-coreml nvidia/diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2 CC BY 4.0 Streaming Sortformer 4spk v2.1 mattt/diar-streaming-sortformer-4spk-v2.1-coreml nvidia/diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2.1 NVIDIA Open Model License Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model. Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools. Speaker diarization When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline: let diarizer = SpeakerDiarizer (model: SortformerDiarizationModel ()) if let request = try await AssetInventory .assetInstallationRequest( supporting: [transcriber, diarizer] ) { try await request.downloadAndInstall() } let analyzer = SpeechAnalyzer (modules: [transcriber, diarizer]) The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today. The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1 , which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too. How well does it work? We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes: Transcriber test-clean test-other Parakeet v3, file 1.55% 2.78% Parakeet v3, live 4.73% 4.29% Parakeet Ultra, file 1.66% 2.55% Parakeet Ultra, live 2.65% 3.28% Parakeet Unified, file 1.43% 2.19% Parakeet Unified, live 1.45% 2.42% Apple's transcriber, file 2.12% 3.97% Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%. These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements . So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone. Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27. AnyDecisionModel AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly. It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification. What's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them. Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives. Here's what a decision looks like in Swift: import AnyDecisionModel enum Department : String , Choosable { case billing, technical, sales } let ticket = "I was charged twice for my order, and now the app logs me out when I try to ask for a refund." let model = MLXDecisionModel (modelID: "mlx-community/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-4bit" ) let session = DecisionSession (model: model, state: .text(ticket)) let urgent = try await session.probability(of: "Does this convey urgency?" ) let team = try await session.choice( "Which team?" , from: Department . self ) let anger = try await session.score( "How frustrated?" , levels: [ "Calm" , "Frustrated" , "Very angry" ] ) urgent is a Double . team is a Choice<Department> containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable , team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch . If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch. For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass. Try it out: Emoji Magnet Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back. The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example: Statement: a heavy winter coat fits the description "things you wear". Is this statement true? The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY , the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive. Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository. Decision heads and Clef Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant. AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX: let model = MLXHeadDecisionModel ( modelID: "mlx-community/clef-flash-4bit" , head: .jointSchema ) You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states. Calibrating and checking probabilities Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration , which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results. Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation. Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere. Backends AnyDecisionModel has six backends: MLX runs a small language model on Apple silicon with mlx-swift-lm and downloads it from the Hub. MLX decision heads run a model with its own trained decision head, such as Clef. Core AI does the same as MLX with a Core AI model on macOS 27 and iOS 27. llama.cpp reads decisions from a local GGUF model through llama.swift . Jev calls TypeSafe's Jev through the System One API , or any server that implements it, such as Kev . Ollama calls a System One decision model on a local Ollama server or in Ollama's cloud. It requires Ollama 0.35.0 or later, or 0.40.5 or later for cloud models. The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit. Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX , CoreAI , or Llama trait for the local backends. Get started Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime. Add the packages to your Package.swift : dependencies: [ .package(url: "https://github.com/mattt/AnySpeechRecognizer" , from: "0.1.0" ), .package( url: "https://github.com/mattt/AnyDecisionModel" , from: "0.6.0" , traits: [ "MLX" ] ), ] For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x. Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear , that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple , --backend parakeet , or --backend qwen ; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets. Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories. content: In Brief Posted: 10:54 AM PDT · October 29, 2026 Image Credits: Granola Ivan Mehta Granola crunches up a dictation feature to compete with Wispr Apps in the consumer voice AI world seem to be converging, as Granola , known for its meeting notetaker, launched a dictation feature today. This comes months after Wispr, known for its dictation tool, launched a meeting notetaker . Granola’s dictation currently works on Mac just like any other such tool. Users can press the “Fn” key and start speaking, and the tool cleans up and formats their speech and posts the final text. This feature works across all apps, so users can post notes, dictate prompts, and reply to emails and messages. The startup said that dictation is available for all plans without any limits. Granola now does voice typing. Unlimited words, for free. Granola already writes your meeting notes. Now it can do the typing for you, in any app. pic.twitter.com/et60VtwWA0 — Granola (@meetgranola) October 29, 2026 The company said that the feature will land on iOS and Windows soon. Granola and Wispr are valued at $1.5 billion and $2 billion , respectively. Granola is focused on meeting-related automation and notetaking. On the other hand, Wispr is trying to build its own models through a research lab, which is exploring different human-computer interfaces. The feature mashups are not exclusive to Granola and Wispr. Other voice startups such as Fireflies , Speechify , and Monologue have converged into multifeature apps with meeting notetaking and dictation capabilities. Until earlier in the year, the play was around having a focused app that does one thing well. But now, all of these apps are thinking about how to get more out of capturing users’ speech. title: Rivian expands joint venture with VW to include AI assistant
description: Rivian doesn't disclose if the value of its $5.8 billion joint venture will expand as a result.
content: The $5.8 billion joint venture between Rivian and Volkswagen Group is expanding to include AI assistants. Rivian is now licensing elements of its AI voice assistant technology to Volkswagen Group as part of the broader joint venture, according to the company’s third-quarter investor presentation released Thursday. Rivian didn’t disclose the licensing fees, payment terms, or which Volkswagen vehicles will use the technology. However, the AI assistant, which recently rolled out to Riv i an vehicles , could make its Volkswagen debut in the automaker’s low-cost EV called the ID EVERY1 . The small four-door hatchback is slated to be the first VW vehicle to use Rivian’s software and electrical architecture under the joint venture established in 2024. The joint venture between Rivian and VW Group has already expanded once before, at least financially. The companies initially announced a joint venture valued up to $5 billion , but within months VW upped its commitment to invest up to $5.8 billion in Rivian by 2027. The initial tie-up, formalized through an independent company that kicked off in November 2024, focused on bringing Rivian’s electrical architecture and software to Volkswagen’s next generation of vehicles. Rivian described the expansion to include elements of its AI assistant technology as “a proof point for the extensibility of the platform we’ve built in-house.” Rivian spent two years developing its AI assistant before showing it off last year. That development work continued longer than expected, with the assistant finally rolling out in May 2026 to its flagship R1S SUV, R1T pickup truck, and in October to its new midsize R2 SUV. Rivian has big aspirations for its AI assistant, which allows drivers and passengers to interact with the vehicle and control certain functions. Rivian founder and CEO RJ Scaringe told TechCrunch onstage at Disrupt 2026 that the company has created its own in-house agentic framework that understands what action a person wants to take when they talk to the vehicle, and routes it to the right part of the car’s software. That capability could eventually allow Rivian vehicles to run AI agents created by other companies, including Anthropic. The in-house AI assistant program also fits into Rivian’s push to become more vertically integrated — a strategy the company emphasized in its third-quarter earnings report. “Our relentless focus on vertical integration remains a core competitive differentiator, allowing Rivian to seamlessly unify our hardware and software architecture to deliver significant value to our customers,” the company noted in its investor presentation. That strategy led to Rivian overhauling its flagship R1T truck and R1S SUV , changing everything from the battery pack and suspension system to the electrical architecture, sensor stack, and software user interface. Its new electric architecture system and compute platform slashed the amount of wiring used and reduced the total number of electronic control units, or computers, used to control the vehicle from 17 different ECUs to seven. That foundation, Rivian argued, would allow it to build vehicles that can handle the computing demands required for advanced software and automated driving. That technology caught the attention (and money) of VW, which has struggled to offer customers a modern software-centric vehicle found in competitors like Tesla. Rivian made that vertical-integration case repeatedly in its investor presentation, noting that because it controls the entire technology stack, including compute, sensors, displays, lighting, and sound, “it can roll out rapid, vehicle-wide OTA updates that go well beyond the basics.” This article was updated to provide the two separate rollout dates for the AI assistant.
