content: The race to build the winning AI assistant is on, and investors are spreading out their bets. On Thursday, another AI app, Wabi , now describing itself as a “personal agent,” said it has raised $55 million at a $1.25 billion valuation. Founded by Eugenia Kuyda, who previously founded the AI companion startup Replika, Wabi originally focused on allowing anyone to build apps using prompts . Last month, however, the startup announced a pivot of sorts to become an AI messenger. The idea now is that the new Wabi — or Wabi 2.0, as it was called — could build the interfaces you need to get things done as part of its role as your personal AI agent. The company suggests Wabi could be used to build mini apps for things like meal planning, tracking local restaurants, planning date nights, creating fitness plans, designing specialized trivia games, and more. Image Credits: Wabi The additional funding indicates that Wabi’s investors agree that its new agentic angle has some potential, especially given the market around AI agents is hot right now, with viral AI agent Instinct pulling in another billion at a $10 billion valuation in September. Even Tolan, which makes a cute, Muppet-like AI companion to help people navigate life, just raised $30 million . “Eugenia has a unique sense for where AI is headed and a track record of great taste in building it,” said Alex Lim, general partner at IVP, which led the new round, in a statement. “She has a clear vision for how people will interact with AI, one that goes far beyond the text box or command line. Wabi is the expression of that vision, and we’re thrilled to support her.” Other participants in the round included Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), Forerunner, Amazon Alexa Fund, and angel investors like Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff, former Yahoo! head Marissa Mayer, former Twitter CEO Dick Costolo, and one half of The Chainsmokers, Alex Pall. title: Ex-Palantir execs launch Dream with $17M from a16z to build AI world models for construction
description: Dream is grounded in real physics and construction standards. Just as LLMs learn from text, Dream's world model is trained on more than 100 million square feet of building data gathered from permit archives across the United States.
content: Andy Elder and Arjun Mathur were Stanford roommates who both studied computer science before spending a decade at Palantir. Elder led product design for a team of 800 people building software for U.S. defense and intelligence agencies, while Mathur served as a senior vice president in the company’s commercial practice. When the friends decided to build a startup early last year, there was no question they would do it together. Despite having no direct background in architecture, Elder and Mathur were troubled by a growing problem: Fewer buildings are constructed in the U.S. today than a few decades ago , as development costs have surged. “We’ve gone from dial-up internet to superintelligent AI, but our ability to build the physical world around us has actually decreased,” Mathur told TechCrunch. Believing AI can boost productivity across the architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC) industry, they set out to build Dream , a startup developing built world models that automate building design and engineering. Dream has emerged from stealth with $17 million in seed funding led by Andreessen Horowitz, alongside other backers, including SV Angel, XYZ, and Zigg Capital. The startup aims to replace cumbersome, outdated AEC tools like Autodesk’s AutoCAD and Revit. If you sit next to an architect or a structural engineer, you’ll notice that they are still “drawing” every piece of their designs part by part on legacy software, Mathur said. “AI really plays no role in that equation.” While a standard LLM like ChatGPT can generate an image of a building, the result won’t be structurally sound. Dream, by contrast, is grounded in real physics and construction standards. Just as LLMs learn from text, Dream’s world model is trained on more than 100 million square feet of building data gathered from permit archives across the United States. “Our model actually understands what’s within those walls. What materials are used, what the beams are made of, and how much weight they can support,” Elder said. The startup calls its approach “structural cognition” because its model generates structurally precise designs that account for internal building elements like plumbing and HVAC. Dream has already begun selling its product to AEC professionals and developers, who use the model to conceptualize building designs and estimate overall costs, according to the founders. The platform is already deployed across 10 active projects in Texas and California. While Dream isn’t the only company attempting to update AEC software with AI — other startups working on this include Motif , Snaptrude , and Arcol — Elder and Mathur claim that they are the only ones that developed a world model that instantly designs whole buildings. Kimberly Tan, a partner at Andreessen Horowitz, said that while the firm first invested in Dream over a year ago, when the startup model was just an idea, she has been extremely impressed with their progress. “I have not seen anybody take the technical approach,” she said. “They’re doing everything based on their own models.” Topics AI , Andreessen Horowitz , architecture , dream , Palantir , Startups , Venture , world models When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . title: Anthropic’s business plan: Build God or die trying
description: The Anthropic S-1 seems to have provided the financial justification for the company to spend as much as it possibly can on compute. If you are the kind of person who wonders if Anthropic is doing its level best to build a machine god while convincing Wall Street it's in the business of selling IT […]
content: AI Business Report Anthropic’s business plan: Build God or die trying Anthropic faces intense competitive pressure and huge fixed costs. Can Claude build itself fast enough to succeed? by Elizabeth Lopatto Oct 29, 2026, 1:30 PM UTC Image: The Verge / Getty Images AI Business Report Anthropic’s business plan: Build God or die trying Anthropic faces intense competitive pressure and huge fixed costs. Can Claude build itself fast enough to succeed? by Elizabeth Lopatto Oct 29, 2026, 1:30 PM UTC Elizabeth Lopatto is a reporter who writes about tech, money, and human behavior. She joined The Verge in 2014 as science editor. Previously, she was a reporter at Bloomberg. The Anthropic S-1 seems to have provided the financial justification for the company to spend as much as it possibly can on compute. If you are the kind of person who wonders if Anthropic is doing its level best to build a machine god while convincing Wall Street it’s in the business of selling IT contracts, Anthropic has just offered a handy solution: Doing a bunch of things that look like you’re trying to build the machine god is the only way to avoid going bankrupt. Forget about the machine god for a minute. At least in my read of the S-1, it seems like Anthropic is pinning the future of its company to dramatic growth; it has to, in order to meet its fixed costs. You don’t have to be an AI skeptic to lift an eyebrow at these numbers. But if you are skeptical that dramatic recursive self-improvement is possible — in the way the business plan seems to require — this doesn’t look like a good investment. Let’s start with the good news for Anthropic fans. The company’s revenue grew fourteen times to $16.3 billion between the first half of 2026 and the first half of 2025. There’s an $80 billion loss, but it’s largely an accounting thing that isn’t relevant to the underlying business . If we remove that, and some other charges, including employee compensation, we’re looking at $1.62 billion in adjusted income in the first half of 2026. I’ve asked before if AI can make enough money to pay for itself , and the answer from Anthropic’s S-1 appears to be, at least for this company, at least right now, yes. Anthropic names only OpenAI and Google as rivals Anthropic was considerably more disciplined than OpenAI or Elon Musk, and it seems to be paying off. (Anthropic names only OpenAI and Google as rivals. Better luck next time, Elon!) The company has never released an AI image generator, an AI TikTok clone, or an AI waifu. Instead, it specialized in tasks like coding and cybersecurity, staying laser-focused on the thing it is easiest for a computer to do: more computer. And it focused on the enterprise market, which is less fickle than consumers. Its net revenue retention is 900 percent. Pretty good! That revenue isn’t consumers, either. About three-quarters of customers in the first half of 2026 are spending at least $100,000 a year. On the other hand, Anthropic is under intense competitive pressure — from both other frontier labs and open-source models. The other frontier labs are all rushing for the cutting edge, too. Claude Opus 5.5 currently sits atop the Epoch Capabilities Index , but that leaderboard changes frequently. And for anyone who doesn’t care that their software is four months behind , there are the open-source ones. What’s more, Anthropic has a disadvantage against a rival like Google. It doesn’t have multiple paths to revenue — and Google does. Google can also wrap its AI into other products businesses already use. Remember when Microsoft Teams ate Slack ? It wasn’t because Teams was the better product; Microsoft just had better distribution, since Teams was bundled with other programs companies were already paying for. Having the best model matters more for cybersecurity — one area Anthropic is targeting for growth — than for instant messaging software, but it’s hard to compete on distribution. There are some long-term commitments that highlight how intense the expansion pressure is on Anthropic And also, revenue comes in spurts, usually after a new model is released. Between the competition and growth in use after each novel model, Anthropic can never stop training, and it has to do so more efficiently than its much larger competition. So one important question is: Can Anthropic continue to provide the results we see in the S-1? There are some long-term commitments that highlight how intense the expansion pressure is on Anthropic. Sure, there’s a convenient blank on its purchase commitments and lease agreements on page 64, and another kicky little blank on the amounts it’s expecting to spend before December 31st, 2030, on page 137. However, we know the commitments run through 2045. Fortunately, there’s a “Commitments and contingencies” section that can help us out a little. There’s a fixed minimum of non-cancelable purchase commitments that total $265.6 billion, with terms between one and 20 years. The company has lease agreements “primarily related to compute and infrastructure capacity” that haven’t yet commenced of $321.4 billion, as of the unaudited June 30th figures. After that, Anthropic entered new compute and infrastructure agreements totaling about $245 billion, again with terms between one and 20 years. There’s some other transactions that haven’t yet been finalized, which Anthropic estimates as costing $125 billion to $150 billion. There are also other compute commitments that are variable. “The S-1 does freeze in time a happy period when their initial models skyrocketed in usage.” If I add all that up, I’m looking at a minimum of around $850 billion of commitments over the next 20 years, which will rise to about a trillion dollars if the transactions that haven’t been finalized are added in at the current estimated cost. And that’s assuming I’m not missing anything, which I may very well be. So to meet those commitments, Anthropic’s growth must continue at breakneck speed. Anthropic doesn’t give us a payment schedule for its future commitments, but analyst Harrison Rolfes of PitchBook models it at about $90 billion a year from 2027 to 2030, which means $188 billion in revenue to keep the current ratio of cost to compute stable. “Growth is not optional for this company,” he writes. “The contracts assume it.” Compute and infrastructure (and a few other items) associated with customers cost $2.3 billion in the first half of this year. Model development (and a few other items) was significantly more expensive; Anthropic spent $9.7 billion on it. But Anthropic simultaneously got more efficient — spending less money on compute to bring in each dollar of revenue, according to Rolfes. Everyone in cybersecurity has to keep running just to stay in the same place, exactly like Anthropic Is that a long-standing trend? Hard to say. We don’t have the third quarter numbers in front of us. “The S-1 does freeze in time a happy period when their initial models skyrocketed in usage and they didn’t have enough compute so they are able to charge more for what they had,” says Brendan Burke, an analyst at Futurum Group. As enterprise software, it makes sense for Anthropic to target companies’ IT budgets. Conveniently, cybersecurity is a place where you will absolutely get your shit rekt if you are not constantly up to date — everyone there has to keep running just to stay in the same place, exactly like Anthropic . Of course, AI is part of the problem; hackers can use it to brute-force stuff they couldn’t do before. Plus, the products themselves are also causing headaches thanks to a partner’s sloppy fuck-up of security protocols around AI agents. Frontier labs need high-margin products to avoid a race to the bottom on token pricing, notes Burke. That made something else stand out to me: Opus 5.5 reduced customer costs by 40 percent over Opus 5. Now, Anthropic says that lower cost means more usage, which lets the company preserve its margins. If you assume that cost reduction happens every time a new model is released, pretty soon you wind up with tasks at a fraction of the price. Claude is already building Claude under human direction This isn’t necessarily an insurmountable problem, in part because increased efficiency doesn’t always slash margins, says Gil Luria, an analyst with DA Davidson. Amazon Web Services and other cloud providers ”have become far more efficient every year and reduce their prices every year and they have had steady growth and rising margins,” he says. But the pressure for growth is pretty undeniable. That’s where recursive self-improvement, with minimal or no supervision, comes in. “More capable models help our researchers discover these improvements faster; in turn, more powerful compute multipliers enable us to train even more capable models and deploy them more efficiently.” Based on the general rhetoric Anthropic has about the apocalypse or whatever, it expects to hit dramatic recursive self-improvement, maybe soon. Claude is already building Claude under human direction. In its risk factors, Anthropic warns that it’s locked in to that approach. That comes with a clear tradeoff, since using AI to develop more AI “may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures.” If I am reading that right, Anthropic is saying that its business relies on building new models so fast, using work it may not fully understand, that it is essentially forced, for business reasons, to do stuff that may be risky to everyone. Which is why we’ve got a bunch of weird stuff about the existential hazards of “catastrophic” harm and the development of “forms of sentience” in the risk factors. Is dramatic recursive self-improvement that escapes the bounds of human supervision possible? Dunno. But if it isn’t, that makes it much harder for Anthropic to meet its existing compute commitments and turn a profit. content: Meta has quietly launched Style Sketch , an AI fashion app that helps users put together outfit ideas using clothes they already own. The app connects to Instagram to build a virtual closet from photos you’ve posted, or lets you add items manually by snapping a photo, recording a quick video, or uploading images from your camera roll. Style Sketch then suggests outfit combinations built from your wardrobe matched to your style. Users can then try on the outfits on a “realistic model matched to your body shape and skin tone,” the app description reads. The app, which was first spotted by social media consultant Matt Navarra , is available in Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand on iOS and Android . Meta did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment. It’s unknown whether Meta plans to launch Style Sketch more widely. 🚨 Meta quietly launched an AI fashion app! 👗 Style Sketch connects to Facebook & Instagram to build a wardrobe from photos you’ve already posted • 👕 AI outfits from clothes you own • 🪞 Virtual try-ons matched to your body • ☀️ Weather-based looks • ✈️ Trip packing plans pic.twitter.com/uNYX6VHRCn — Matt Navarra (@MattNavarra) October 28, 2026 Several apps already use AI to help users digitize their wardrobes and visualize new outfits, including startups like Alta . Even Google Photos offers tools that let users turn photos of their clothes into digital closets where they can create new outfit ideas. To compete with what’s already on the market, Meta will likely rely less on the novelty of the idea and more on the app’s integration with Instagram, where users already have a visual record of their personal style. Rather than relying on random suggestions, users can also select a specific item from their wardrobe and get fresh outfit ideas built around it, according to the app description. The app can also help users plan outfits for trips. If they enter their destination, trip length, and planned activities, users can get a day-by-day outfit plan that takes the weather forecast and itinerary into account. Style Sketch is one of many AI apps from Meta in recent months. Most recently, the company launched an app called Waddle World , which essentially looks like a Tamagotchi clone, but with AI. Meta has also launched Pocket , a tool for vibe-coding games, and Vibes , which lets users quickly generate AI-powered videos. The wave of new apps is part of a broader effort at Meta to release more apps. The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this year that CEO Mark Zuckerberg told employees the company plans to release far more apps than it has historically, as AI-driven efficiencies have made it faster and easier to ship new apps.
